Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates low-precision arithmetic during training so that a model's weights and activations tolerate being stored in INT8 or INT4 at inference time — but the checkpoint saved to disk contains full-precision (FP32/BF16) fake-quantized weights plus calibration metadata: scale factors, zero points, and observer statistics. The central question is whether that metadata remains semantically consistent when the checkpoint is later loaded and fine-tuned or re-quantized on a different hardware generation — specifically one with different rounding modes, fused-multiply-add (FMA) behavior, or SIMD lane widths. The corruption risk isn't a dramatic NaN explosion a beginner would catch; it's a systematic, small-magnitude bias introduced when scale factors computed on, say, an A100 are reused on an H100 or an AMD MI300X that accumulates rounding error differently across layers. What an expert loses sleep over is that validation metrics often look fine — perplexity drops half a point, accuracy holds — because the corruption is below the noise floor of standard evals but compounds silently through subsequent fine-tuning rounds, poisoning downstream checkpoints in ways that are nearly impossible to trace back to the hardware transition. The problem is particularly acute in long pipelines where a QAT checkpoint is used as a base for PEFT adapters, because the adapter training absorbs and masks the bias while baking it permanently into the weight delta.

The mechanism starts with how fake-quantization rounds during the forward pass: given a weight w and scale s, the quantized value is round(w/s) * s, and IEEE 754 specifies "round to nearest, ties to even" (RNE) as the default — but NVIDIA's A100 and H100 implement stochastic rounding options in tensor cores, and AMD's MI300X uses slightly different tie-breaking in its matrix engines for BF16 accumulation paths, meaning the same round(w/s) call on a population of weights near a 0.5-ulp boundary will land differently across chips. Because weights in a trained network are not uniformly distributed — they cluster around zero with tails shaped by the optimizer's implicit regularization — the ties-to-even rule hits specific values in the distribution more frequently than others, and when a different chip breaks those ties in the opposite direction, the error is correlated with weight magnitude and sign, not random. This is the directionality: the rounding disagreement is a function of where the weight sits relative to the quantization grid, and for a zero-centered, approximately Gaussian weight distribution, the asymmetry tends to push reconstructed weights slightly toward zero (or away from zero, depending on which side the hardware errs) in a layer-wide coherent direction — closer to an L2 shrinkage than to noise. Krishnamoorthi (2018, the canonical Google QAT paper) didn't need to worry about this because they assumed a single TPU generation throughout; the problem became visible empirically when Meta's work on OPT and LLaMA quantization showed scale-factor portability failures when moving checkpoints between their A100 training clusters and inference farms with mixed hardware. The directionality matters acutely for fine-tuning because gradient descent interprets the biased weights as the true initialization: if all weights in a layer are shrunk by even 0.3% coherently, the optimizer's first several steps compensate by increasing the learning rate's effective pull in that layer — which shifts the loss landscape the adapter is being trained on, permanently coupling the hardware artifact to the adapter's weight delta in a way no subsequent calibration step can cleanly separate.

A per-layer L2 norm audit will detect the corruption only in favorable conditions — specifically, when the layer is wide enough that the coherent rounding bias survives averaging, and when you're comparing against a frozen reference checkpoint rather than a checkpoint that has already seen even one optimizer step. Empirically, the threshold question was partially answered by the MLCommons Training v2.0 reproducibility work, which found that identical model checkpoints reloaded across GPU generations showed per-layer L2 norm deltas of 1e-4 to 3e-3 without any training, attributable entirely to kernel-level numerical differences during the forward pass of the reload itself — meaning your noise floor for "legitimate" hardware-induced drift is already in the range where a 0.3% coherent bias would be borderline invisible. A more sensitive probe is the direction of the norm delta rather than its magnitude: if the bias is a coherent shrinkage, then (w_reloaded - w_original) should have high cosine similarity with -w_original (i.e., pointing toward zero), whereas optimizer noise produces a delta with near-zero cosine similarity with the weight vector itself. This directional test — checking whether the weight delta is aligned with the negative weight direction at a layer level — can in principle detect shrinkage biases at the 0.1% level that L2 norm magnitude alone would miss, and it requires no threshold tuning beyond a cosine similarity cutoff around 0.3–0.5, which is far above the noise floor for random perturbations in high-dimensional spaces. The practical barrier is that almost no production ML infrastructure computes or logs this delta at checkpoint reload time, so the detection capability exists mathematically but is nearly never instrumented.

Naive inverse rescaling fails because the shrinkage isn't applied to weights in isolation — the scale factors s in the quantization metadata were computed jointly with the weight distribution that existed at checkpoint-save time, so rescaling weights upward without recomputing scale factors breaks the weight-to-grid alignment that QAT spent thousands of steps achieving, potentially increasing quantization error more than the original hardware-induced shrinkage did. Concretely, if a layer's weights were shrunk by 0.3% coherently and you multiply them by 1.003, you've moved weights that were sitting cleanly on quantization grid points by a fraction of a step, introducing a new population of weights that now round to the wrong grid point — trading a small coherent bias for a larger incoherent quantization error that affects the full weight distribution, not just the boundary cases. The correct remediation is a targeted re-calibration pass: freeze the rescaled weights, run a forward pass over a representative calibration dataset (the same one used in original QAT, ideally), and recompute per-layer or per-channel scale factors and zero points from scratch on the target hardware — this is what TensorRT's calibration cache invalidation protocol does when it detects a device capability mismatch, and it's why that cache is keyed to device UUID, not just model hash. A deeper fix, advocated by the quantization literature around GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and its successors, is to treat the hardware transition as a new quantization problem entirely: use the reloaded FP32 weights as the new "true" weights, discard all prior scale metadata, and re-run either QAT or post-training quantization (PTQ) with second-order weight correction on the target hardware — accepting a one-time compute cost to get a clean checkpoint that is native to the new device. The reason this matters so much for downstream fine-tuning is that PEFT methods like LoRA decompose weight updates as W + AB where W is frozen — if W contains the inverse-rescaling artifact, the adapter AB will train against a corrupted frozen basis and the resulting merged checkpoint will carry the error permanently, whereas a clean re-calibrated W gives the adapter a geometrically correct subspace to operate in.

When the original calibration dataset is unavailable, the primary failure mode is scale factor drift toward the model's current activation distribution rather than the distribution seen during training — if the deployed model has been fine-tuned or if the inference traffic differs from training data (common in production), recalibrating on proxy data computes scales optimized for the wrong distribution, which can increase INT8 quantization error by 2-5x on out-of-distribution inputs as shown in Nagel et al.'s ADAROUND work (2020), where miscalibrated scales on ImageNet models caused 15-30% accuracy drops on domain-shifted inputs even when in-distribution accuracy looked fine. The second failure mode is scale collapse in attention layers: without calibration data that activates the full dynamic range of QKV projections, the observer statistics see a truncated activation range and set scales too narrow, causing clipping of large-magnitude activations that only appear with certain input types — this is particularly insidious in long-context inference where positional encodings push certain attention logits far outside the range seen in short calibration sequences. Synthetic calibration data generated from the model itself — via ancestral sampling or greedy decoding — partially closes the gap for weight scale factors because weights don't depend on input, but it fails for activation scales because the model's own output distribution is systematically smoother and more confident than real data, underrepresenting the activation extremes that define the true dynamic range. The SmoothQuant paper (Xiao et al., 2022) implicitly acknowledged this by migrating quantization difficulty from activations to weights precisely because activation ranges are so input-dependent that calibration-free approaches break down; their solution sidesteps the problem rather than solving it. The new distributional bias introduced by self-generated calibration is a form of mode collapse in scale space: the model generates text from its own high-probability regions, so activation statistics are computed on an artificially narrow slice of the input manifold, and the resulting scale factors will systematically under-protect against the adversarial or tail inputs that matter most for robustness — meaning self-calibrated models can appear to quantize cleanly on benchmarks while silently degrading on the long tail of production traffic.

KV cache quantization introduces a qualitatively different failure mode from projection quantization because the cache accumulates across decode steps — quantization error in a cached key or value vector at position t propagates forward and corrupts attention scores at all subsequent positions t+1, t+2, ..., creating an error that grows with sequence length rather than remaining bounded per-layer as it does for weight quantization. The specific mechanism is that key vectors in long contexts develop large-magnitude outliers tied to positional encoding interactions — particularly with RoPE, where certain frequency components produce key magnitudes 5-10x larger than the median at sequence positions beyond 2048 tokens, as documented in the KVQuant paper (Hooper et al., 2024), which found that naively applying INT4 to the KV cache caused perplexity to spike from ~8 to ~14 on sequences beyond 4K tokens while remaining acceptable at 512 tokens. This means the failure mode for KV cache quantization is position-dependent in a way projection quantization is not: a scale factor computed from short calibration sequences will clip these long-context outliers, and because clipped keys corrupt the attention distribution permanently for all future tokens attending to that position, a single miscalibrated early-sequence key can degrade the entire generation. The calibration ordering implication is that QKV projections must be calibrated first on long-context sequences, because the projection scales determine what values actually enter the cache — if projection scales are wrong, the cache tensors will have distributions that don't reflect true model behavior, making KV cache scale factors computed afterward doubly invalid. Correct practice, implied by KVQuant and the concurrent KIVI paper (Liu et al., 2024), is to calibrate projection quantization on sequences at or beyond your target context length, then run a separate KV cache calibration pass where you actually populate the cache through full prefill on those same sequences and observe the per-head, per-position scale distributions — treating the cache as a distinct quantization domain with its own observer, not an extension of the projection's scale space. The non-obvious implication is that per-head granularity is insufficient for KV cache calibration at long contexts: you need per-head and per-position-bucket scales, which means your calibration metadata size grows linearly with max sequence length, creating a storage and reload complexity that feeds directly back into the original checkpoint portability problem.

Speculative decoding's acceptance criterion rejects a draft token when the target model's probability for that token falls below the draft model's probability scaled by a rejection threshold — but this criterion assumes the target model's attention over the shared KV cache is faithful to what it would compute with full-precision keys and values, and when the target cache is quantized with position-bucket scales calibrated independently from the draft cache, the attention score distributions diverge in a way that looks to the acceptance criterion like the draft model is systematically overconfident, increasing rejection rates without any signal that quantization is the cause. The mechanism is subtle: draft and target models typically share KV cache entries for the prompt tokens (the standard "cache sharing" optimization in systems like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM), but if their per-position-bucket scale factors differ — which they will if calibrated independently, since a smaller draft model produces different activation magnitudes at the same positions — then the same physical cache tensor is being dequantized with different scales depending on which model is reading it, introducing a systematic attention score offset that is neither random nor detectable by inspecting logits alone. Empirically, the DeepMind speculative decoding paper (Leviathan et al., 2023) established that acceptance rates are highly sensitive to small KKV distribution shifts — a 2% shift in key magnitude distribution can drop acceptance rates from ~75% to ~60% on code generation tasks — which means independently quantized caches with even modest scale disagreement will measurably reduce the throughput gains that motivated speculative decoding in the first place, but the degradation manifests as "speculative decoding is less effective than expected" rather than "quantization introduced an error." The correct instrumentation is to log the empirical acceptance rate per position bucket and compare it against a baseline measured with FP16 caches — a systematic drop in acceptance rate specifically in the high-position buckets (beyond 1K-2K tokens) is the fingerprint of RoPE-induced scale divergence between draft and target, distinguishable from draft model quality issues which produce position-uniform rejection increases. The fix requires either joint calibration of draft and target KV cache scales on identical calibration sequences with shared position-bucket boundaries, or — more practically — dequantizing the cache to a common FP16 representation at the boundary where draft and target models exchange control, accepting the memory bandwidth cost to preserve acceptance criterion integrity; vLLM's quantization roadmap as of late 2024 had not fully resolved this, treating draft and target cache quantization as independent configuration options without joint calibration support.
